title: What Big Companies Can Learn from Breakout Brands
gist: US consumer packaged goods manufacturers under $1 billion in measured retail sales are generating the majority of category growth, because creators, marketplaces, specialty retail and AI-powered discovery let brands like Lemme, Boka and Recess reach scale before mass awareness. The diagnosis is structural rather than a talent gap: risk asymmetry, materiality, coordination and diffuse brand ownership stop multinationals from reinventing or scaling brands, and the prescribed fixes are ring-fencing midsize brands, sequencing distribution behind velocity, paying creators a cut of sales, and running AI native.

insights.claim: Women's health and supplement brand Lemme passed $200 million in sales within four years of launching a $30 gummy priced well above the category average, while its brand awareness among US consumers remained under 10%.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Revenue has decoupled from awareness, so screening emerging consumer brands on awareness or ad spend will systematically miss the fastest compounders.
insights.locator: When Nir Liberboim and his cofounders launched Lemme

insights.claim: US consumer packaged goods manufacturers that earned less than $1 billion in measured retail sales generated the majority of category growth, according to NielsenIQ data.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Category growth is migrating below the $1 billion revenue line, which argues for exposure to emerging-brand platforms and aggregators over large-cap staples incumbents.
insights.locator: The clearest casualties are midsize brands

insights.claim: Digital marketplaces, creators, specialty retail, social commerce and AI-powered discovery let brands aggregate pockets of intense consumer demand before achieving mass awareness, so meaningful scale arrives much earlier than the traditional build-awareness-then-distribution model predicts.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The cost curve of brand building has shifted; paid-media scale is no longer the moat it was for incumbents.
insights.locator: Understanding how breakout brands grow is the first step

insights.claim: Barriers to entry in consumer brands are as low as they have ever been because a founder can outsource almost every function and reach the shelf needing little of the infrastructure the industry once demanded.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Low entry costs mean brand supply keeps rising and differentiation, not infrastructure, is the scarce asset worth paying for.
insights.quote: The barriers to entry are as low as ever. Retailers are there. Amazon is there. Marketing is there.
insights.locator: It's relatively easy to start a brand today

insights.claim: The scaling gap bites at both ends of a portfolio: large brands lose share because company systems are built to defend rather than reinvent them, and midsize brands stall because they are too big to fly under the radar and too small to command the attention of a large company's branding machines.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Midsize brands trapped inside large portfolios are the likeliest divestiture or carve-out candidates and a source of mispriced assets.
insights.locator: It shows up at both ends of a portfolio

insights.claim: Brands that beat incumbents did so by delighting people more rather than by positioning as challengers, and the labels challenger and disruptive were applied only by the companies being disrupted.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Incumbent framing of upstarts as challengers is a tell that management misdiagnoses the threat as positioning rather than product experience.
insights.quote: No human being has ever said, ‘Next time you are shopping, can you get me some of those challenger products?’
insights.locator: The builders of breakout brands resist the industry's vocabulary

insights.claim: Already a top Amazon seller, Boka entered Walmart and Target in 2025 with two toothpaste SKUs and beat buyer expectations; Othership turned a backyard ice bath into a bathhouse chain across two countries; coffee brand Happy LLC reached 12,000 retail outlets and 60,000 product placements within two years of launch.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Online performance is now a credible substitute for trade history in winning mass retail placement, compressing time from launch to national distribution.
insights.locator: Already a top seller on Amazon, Boka entered Walmart and Target

insights.claim: Risk asymmetry blocks reinvention in large companies: incentives reward stewardship of proven brands, so a small bet that succeeds is immaterial while one that fails is significant, and typical executive tenure rarely accommodates a durable bet.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Absent changed incentive and tenure structures, announced innovation programs at large CPGs should be discounted as unlikely to produce durable new brands.
insights.locator: The first is risk asymmetry

insights.claim: Because a new brand is too small to command senior-leader attention for years, large companies default to M&A, and transaction and overhead costs pull acquirers toward brands that have already proved their business model — a pattern visible in Grüns and rhode each selling for about a billion dollars.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect incumbents to keep paying roughly $1 billion for de-risked emerging brands, supporting valuations for late-stage consumer assets with proven repeat purchase.
insights.locator: The second is materiality

insights.claim: Tightly managed channel, price and portfolio decisions create such internal complexity inside large CPG companies that by the time decisions are settled a fast-moving trend has often already passed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Coordination latency is the structural reason incumbents buy trends instead of catching them; decision cycle time is the diagnostic to watch.
insights.locator: The third is coordination

insights.claim: Once a brand is at scale it is maintained by many functions, so the sharp point of view that defined it early gets lost, and the work can be flawless by every professional standard while still failing to connect culturally.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Diffuse ownership, not budget, explains incumbent brand decay — single-owner accountability is the cheap fix to look for in a turnaround.
insights.quote: I show it to my daughter, she says it’s cringe.
insights.locator: The fourth is ownership

insights.claim: Large consumer goods companies are optimization machines for the brands they already own rather than invention machines, and their gap versus startups is structural rather than a shortage of talent or foresight.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Underwrite incumbent CPG on margin and cash extraction from existing brands, not on organic new-brand creation.
insights.quote: Large CPGs work to optimize the brands they have. They are not invention machines.
insights.locator: Why Scaling Works Differently Inside a Multinational

insights.claim: Defining Recess as a relaxation brand rather than a CBD or magnesium beverage company let it survive the pivot away from CBD and stretch across sparkling waters, mocktails and powders.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brands defined by outcome rather than ingredient carry optionality through ingredient-cycle busts — a concrete durability test for consumer bets.
insights.quote: I’ve never heard anyone call Red Bull a caffeine company. It’s an energy drink company. Similarly, I never thought of Recess as a CBD or magnesium beverage company; we were a relaxation brand,
insights.locator: Start with the outcome, not the category

insights.claim: Treating the product as a delivery system for a consumer outcome — coffee as a delivery system for happiness, toothpaste reframed as part of a wellness ritual rather than a chore — is the shared operating principle across breakout brands.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An outcome-defined brand can expand its addressable market without repositioning costs; category-defined brands cannot.
insights.quote: We’re not in the coffee business, we’re in the happy business. Coffee is a delivery system.
insights.locator: Hello's Dubitsky, who also built eos

insights.claim: Consumers hire a brand to do a job at a specific occasion rather than hiring an individual ingredient, which is why a grocery store is best understood as a collection of value propositions rather than a set of categories.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Category share data understates competitive threat, because real competitors are defined by occasion and need state, not shelf adjacency.
insights.quote: Consumers hire a brand to do a job. They’re not hiring an individual ingredient. People seek solutions and brand experiences that fulfill a specific need state at specific occasions.
insights.locator: Witte supplies the logic: What is a grocery store?

insights.claim: Most large-company innovation is narrow line extension rather than the white space founders pursue, yet every founder interviewed also chose a large, growing category, so where to play still matters as much as how.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Incumbent pipelines dominated by line extensions signal a defensive posture; category tailwind remains a precondition even for excellent execution.
insights.locator: Most large-company innovation is narrow

insights.claim: Growth investor Prelude Growth Partners sees roughly a thousand brands a year and invests in roughly two, screening at $10 million to $20 million in sales for two things that must both already be visible: efficient customer acquisition and durable repeat purchasing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete two-variable diligence screen with a roughly 0.2% selection rate: repeat rate plus acquisition efficiency are the only pre-scale metrics that matter.
insights.quote: One side without the other is not enough.
insights.locator: Gain velocity on the shelf, then get distribution

insights.claim: The operating rule multinationals most often break is keeping sales velocity ahead of distribution, and velocity in the existing core category ahead of expansion into new ones.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Distribution growth outrunning velocity is an early warning of shelf churn and markdowns; track velocity per door, not door count.
insights.quote: We want velocity to be ahead of distribution
insights.locator: Her operating rule is the one that multinationals often break

insights.claim: Retailers hungry for growth are now readier than in the past to take on a new brand early and place it in a meaningful number of stores on the strength of its online performance, which makes distribution restraint harder to maintain than it once was.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Easy shelf access is a value trap for young brands: over-distribution risk now exceeds under-distribution risk.
insights.locator: This discipline is harder to maintain than it once was

insights.claim: Lemme sequenced distribution for brand building rather than volume — starting with Ulta shortly after launch, then Target's beauty aisle and premium duty-free shops, with no grocery distribution until year four — and that scarcity earned permanent displays and retailer-funded promotion because a brand that lifts the category's average price is worth more than one more item on the shelf.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Deliberate scarcity converts into retailer-funded economics, a margin lever invisible in headline distribution metrics.
insights.quote: If we’re everywhere, it’s hard to get that level of commitment from our retail partners
insights.locator: Liberboim sequenced Lemme's distribution for brand building

insights.claim: Nurse-led ear-piercing brand Rowan opened three studios in unrelated US markets — Westport, Connecticut; Denver, Colorado; and Alpharetta, Georgia — that each returned their initial capital within months, and the company now runs roughly 115 studios with many customers still thinking it is a local brand.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Payback within months across dissimilar markets is the unit-economics proof that de-risks a rollout; three uncorrelated markets is the minimum test.
insights.quote: We proved the unit economics in three markets that had nothing in common. That is when I knew it would scale.
insights.locator: Louisa Serene Schneider applied this lesson in physical retail

insights.claim: Rowan bought location instead of impressions because a storefront in a top-tier center reaches more people per dollar than a Meta or Google ad.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rising digital ad costs turn prime physical retail into a media buy, not just a sales channel — supportive for top-tier center landlords and store-led brands.
insights.locator: Rather than buy impressions she bought location

insights.claim: Roughly 5,000 creators posted about oral-care brand Boka in the past 18 months despite it paying almost no one for posting, and its social activity generated about a billion views in 2025.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Billion-view reach at near-zero posting spend is the new benchmark; paid-media-dependent brands carry a structural customer-acquisition-cost disadvantage.
insights.locator: Demand is earned, not bought

insights.claim: Creator compensation has shifted from paying per post to paying a cut of sales, and sponsored posts perform poorly because consumers sense the sponsorship.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Performance-linked creator economics move marketing from fixed to variable cost — a margin-structure change worth checking in any consumer P&L.
insights.quote: you have to pay a cut of the sales.
insights.locator: You don't pay by the post anymore

insights.claim: Celebrity fame creates one-time trial but not lasting demand, which is why Bella Hadid's skin parfum brand Orebella avoids megainfluencer fees and excessive paid media and instead leverages her community of 60 million Instagram followers alongside tastemakers, real-life activations and organic AI discovery.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Celebrity-fronted consumer launches should be underwritten on repeat rate, not launch trial; fame is a distribution discount, not a demand engine.
insights.quote: It will get people to try the product once, but it doesn’t create lasting demand.
insights.locator: Celebrity cofounders are often seen as a shortcut in CPG

insights.claim: Beauty brand Saltair says its marketing efficiency has not dropped as community and spending grew — contrary to the usual pattern — because it supplements spending with connection through suburban store appearances, regional influencer get-togethers and consumer pop-ups.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Flat or improving marketing efficiency at scale is rare and is the strongest single signal that a consumer brand's growth is durable rather than bought.
insights.quote: As the community grows and you’re spending more, efficiency usually drops. Ours hasn’t,
insights.locator: Rachel Shelowitz, CEO of Saltair

insights.claim: Saltair is built around its community rather than its founder — most of that community engages without being aware of cofounder Iskra Lawrence — and it follows the consumer onto Discord, TikTok, webinars or in-person meetups because the relationship, not the platform, is the asset.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Community-owned rather than platform-owned or founder-owned demand survives algorithm changes and founder departures — a key durability question in diligence.
insights.quote: The dialogue with the community is the goal; the channel is just where it happens.
insights.locator: The brand is built around its community rather than its founder

insights.claim: Community cannot be manufactured by marketing spend: it forms around a product worth talking about, and no amount of spending holds a community together if the product has not earned it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Marketing budgets cannot substitute for product differentiation; heavy spend behind an undifferentiated product is a warning sign, not a growth signal.
insights.quote: The product itself has to create the community. There’s no amount of marketing or preopening stuff that will sustain community outside of your product experience.
insights.locator: Community cannot be manufactured

insights.claim: Live social selling, where creators sell in live video streams while viewers buy in the moment, is already popular in China and is framed as the next frontier and an incredible unlock for modern brands, but nobody has quite cracked the code yet.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An open, unclaimed channel: first movers in Western live-commerce infrastructure or execution capture an unlock no one has yet taken.
insights.quote: I think that will be an incredible unlock for modern brands, because of the authenticity, because of the founders, because of the storytelling.
insights.locator: Daneshzadeh adds that the next frontier is live social selling

insights.claim: Act one of brand building belongs to industry outsiders — Recess's founder had never met anyone who worked in consumer packaged goods and counts that as the reason he could see the space differently — while act two requires category veterans, with Recess later assembling an executive team drawn from the fastest-growing beverage brands of the past five years.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The founder-to-operator transition is a diagnosable risk; outsider founders who fail to bring in veterans at scale stall.
insights.locator: Talent comes in two stages

insights.claim: Breakout brands hire ahead of revenue on the view that great talent always pays its way quickly, rather than staffing to current scale.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Elevated operating expense ahead of revenue in an emerging brand may be deliberate strategy rather than cost-control failure — read headcount timing accordingly.
insights.quote: great talent always pays its way quickly.
insights.locator: Act two is when CPG veterans become necessary

insights.claim: Essor rebuilt its entire supply chain software stack internally in 12 months, replacing almost every purchased product except its data warehouse, on the reasoning that building is now faster than buying.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If build-beats-buy generalizes, vertical software vendors serving mid-market consumer firms face a structural demand threat while data warehouses look stickier.
insights.locator: Run AI native, not AI curious

insights.claim: Essor abolished the product manager role and embedded engineers in business teams, runs an autonomous agent that surfaces a hundred SEO opportunities every Monday, and requires every new hire to ship an AI project within three months.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete template for AI-native org design — agents inside workflows plus elimination of coordination roles — usable as a checklist against management claims of AI adoption.
insights.locator: It has abolished the product manager role

insights.claim: Lemme runs an AI task force that assesses every function on a monthly basis, and AI-enabled granularity now lets founders see costs and margins down to the individual shipping container at sub-$100 million revenue scale, which was previously impossible.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Small brands now have enterprise-grade cost visibility, eroding a traditional scale advantage of multinationals in procurement and logistics.
insights.quote: We would never have been able to do that for a sub-$100 million company,
insights.locator: Similarly, Lemme has an AI task force

insights.claim: Enterprise AI adoption moves slowly because of procurement and approval layers and legacy stacks that every new tool must accommodate, while startups face far lower barriers — making the speed of embedding AI the clearest observable difference between breakout brands and incumbents.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Legacy stack and procurement drag, not model access, is the binding constraint on enterprise AI returns — a reason to discount incumbent AI narratives.
insights.locator: In our experience, enterprises' adoption of AI moves slowly

insights.claim: AI discovery should be treated as the next shelf, with brands earning a place on it by being worthy of recommendations rather than by buying placement.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If AI assistants become a primary discovery surface, share of recommendation replaces share of shelf as the metric to track for consumer brands.
insights.locator: Rebuild the demand engine around results

themes.theme: Incumbent playbook to close the gap

insights.claim: The prescribed first move for multinationals is to ring-fence emerging brands, running midsize and newly acquired brands on a separate operating system with its own governance, culture and speed, and keeping them independent for far longer than feels comfortable.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Rapid integration of an acquired consumer brand into the parent operating model is a value-destruction signal; delayed integration is the constructive tell.
insights.locator: Five Moves That Can Close the Gap for Multinationals

insights.claim: Emerging brands should be treated as bets — invested in on early visible signs of repeat purchase and momentum but before the brand's value is fully priced — with a few failures accepted as the cost of the winners, and small brands serving as a farm team for the acquirer.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Buying only de-risked brands at billion-dollar prices is the expensive default; earlier, portfolio-style entry is the arbitrage incumbents leave on the table.
insights.quote: A brand like Hello should be a farm team. We could take chances that a large organization can’t afford to take, and if we’re right, they can help us move up to the major league.
insights.locator: Second, treat emerging brands as bets

insights.claim: Putting brand before margin means assigning one owner accountable for the soul of each brand with real authority over product, voice and channel and room to spend when the spreadsheet objects — as when Lemme committed $100,000 to a single custom gummy mold before launch and maintained one price across every channel.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: One price across channels and pre-launch product investment are cheap observable proxies for whether a brand is run for equity or quarterly margin.
insights.locator: Put the brand before the margin

insights.claim: Brands should hold price steady rather than shrink packaging to hit a higher price point, and should not cede the physical theater of permanent and occasion-based displays that brands are now redefining with retailers.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shrinking pack sizes is framed as brand-equity destruction rather than a neutral pricing tool — a negative signal when incumbents lean on it.
insights.locator: Sequence distribution, don't chase it

insights.claim: Midsize brands should be used as the AI laboratory because they are small enough to transform and large enough to prove the business model, run with fewer layers, forward-deployed builders, agents inside workflows and a mandate that every team ships with AI guidance.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Where an incumbent pilots AI reveals seriousness: midsize-brand deployment is a real test, corporate-center pilots usually are not.
insights.locator: Go AI native where the stakes are survivable

insights.claim: Multinationals still own what large-scale brands require — manufacturing capacity, distribution muscle and a balance sheet that founders covet — but lack what startups were forced to learn first: how to launch a brand and earn sales velocity.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The trade is complementarity — incumbent assets plus startup velocity — which keeps acquisition demand structurally high for proven emerging brands.
insights.quote: The dirty little secret is every little company wishes they were a big company.
insights.locator: Multinationals still own what large-scale brands require
